To this dynamic theory Adams added a Law of Acceleration: coal-output doubling every decade, force compounding upon force, the human meteor drawn ever faster toward a perihelion at which the mind itself would have to leap into a new equilibrium or be dissipated.

Nearly forty years after the ex-secretary and his elders had watched the caravan of American society stretch for the plains, he came up the bay again, November 5, 1904, older than either of them had been, to find the approach frantic, wonderful, and repellent. Power had burst its cylinder and flung stone and steam against the sky; the town had the air of hysteria; the citizens cried that the new forces must be mastered, while the forces, condensed into corporations, called for a new man with tenfold endurance and mind, and promised millions to hand. Municipal elections shrieked chaos. At the club window on Fifth Avenue, the traveller thought himself in Rome under Diocletian—anarchy obvious, compulsion clear, the solution demanded—but no Constantine in sight. Two thousand years of Christianity roared their failure from Broadway.

He went on to Washington to wait the end. There Roosevelt, training Constantines, battled Trusts. To a student of mechanics the sympathy was entire, for Trusts were merely the most vigorous expression of the new power since 1840, revolutionary as a liner’s screws to a school of herring, trampling society; while the counter-force behind Roosevelt—generous, moral, but untrained, incoherent, uncertain of its ends—had to create not merely a curb, but the society competent to manage power. If a new American was to appear, he must be the child of the new energies or a sport of nature. The mechanical law seemed to require that mass should rule and progress should continue its acceleration. A nineteenth-century education was as useless in 1904 as the eighteenth had been to the child of 1838, and disputation meant nothing; at such velocity the head of the meteor-stream must soon pass perihelion. Discussion was futile; silence, next to good temper, was sense; the mathematician of 1950 would plot the orbit if the acceleration held.

There, too, life stopped. Nature has a sympathy with death. Seals crawl fifty miles up Antarctic glacier to die in peace, shrinking from marine enemies; Purun Dass, when he had done with statesmanship, sought sanctity among deer and monkeys. Even in America, an Indian Summer should be sunny and sad, not hustled. Obscurity might be nearer nature than Hay’s exposure; the old animal dislikes being worried to death by creatures that have not the teeth to kill him.

On reaching Washington, November 14, 1904, one glance showed that Hay must rest. Mrs. Hay had already marked Europe for relief as soon as the Session ended; Hay protested, and then yielded. For Adams the single vanity worth a martyrdom was to see Hay close by making peace in the East; but Russia fulfilled his formula of inertia with exasperating correctness. Port Arthur fell January 1, 1905; instead of negotiating, she meant to wait till her Baltic fleet should be destroyed; the delay measured precisely the time Hay had left.

March 4 closed the Session; on March 18 he crawled on board ship and revived at sea, gay as when, forty-four years earlier, he had lighted on the Markoe house in I Street. He had no illusions; he talked lightly of the death sentence one might any day expect; the malaria of power passed, leaving only the sense of tasks incomplete.

One could help him there. Laughing at a dozen treaties hung up in the Senate Committee-room like lambs in a butcher’s shop, Adams could count what was finished. In eight years Hay had solved nearly all the old problems; he had brought the great Atlantic powers into a working system; even Russia seemed on the point of being dragged into a combine of intelligent equilibrium, each activity intelligently allotted. For the first time in fifteen hundred years a Roman pax was in sight, and, if it came, it would owe its virtues to him. Except for peace in Manchuria, he could do no more; if the alternative came—continents set against continents in arms—he need not repine at missing the catastrophe.

The Kaiser supplied disturbance enough as the Cretic approached Morocco; chaos waited for the landing. They hid a fortnight at Nervi; Hay gained as long as he made no effort; then they went on to Nauheim. Adams left him there and came to Paris. Reports promised well; Hay’s letters were humorous and sceptical as ever; but when treatment ended, and he came to Paris, he had lost strength. Affairs and interviews wore him out. In their last talk before London and Liverpool he took the end for granted. “You must hold out for the peace negotiations,” said the friend. “I’ve not time!” he answered. “You’ll need little time!” came the rejoinder. Each was correct.

There it ended. “The rest is silence!” A few weeks later, one warm evening in early July, on the way to dine under the trees at Armenonville, Adams learned that Hay was dead. He expected it; he was content that his friend should die, as all would if they could, in full fame at home and abroad, wielding power to the last, spared the cheap obscurity that overtakes emperors and heroes even in life. Not shock, but summons, threw him into Shakespeare’s silence in the flare of Paris frivolity: it was time to go. The three friends had begun together; the last had no motive to carry on after the others. Education had ended, and only beyond a remoter horizon could its values be fixed or renewed. Perhaps in 1938, their centenary, they might return for a holiday, to see their mistakes made clear in the light of their successors’, and, perhaps for the first time since man began his schooling among the carnivores, find a world that timid and sensitive natures could regard without a shudder.
